For Respondents No.1 to 4: Shri HB Agrawal,

Being aggrieved by the order dated 29.08.2017 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge to 1 st Additional Sessions Judge, Durg, District Durg in Criminal Revision No.111/2016 whereby,
upholding the order dated 26.03.2016 passed by JMFC, Durg, an application under Section 156(3)
Cr.P.C was dismissed, the Petitioners have filed this Petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
2.

entities.text: Additional Sessions Judge to 1 st Additional Sessions Judge, Durg, District Durg
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Brief facts of the case are that Respondents No.1 & 2 are the directors of Company working in the name and style of Sanwariya Renewal Energy Solution Limited and Respondents No.3 & 4 are the partners of Shyam Soap Works Factory.
It is alleged that both the factories are adjacent to each other and are situated in the area of 20000 and 18000 sq. ft respectively at village Somani, District Rajnangaon.

It is further alleged that both the factories were given on lease by the District Trade and Teeka Ram Chandel vs Anis on 20 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76709436/
1 Industries Centre, Rajnandgaon (for short 'the DIC') to Respondents No.1 to 4, who have entered into an agreement on 03.06.2014 for taking over the said factories in favour of the Petitioners for a consideration to the tune of Rs.91 lacs out of which, Rs.21,24,000/- was paid in cash as earnest money and it has also been agreed that the Complainant has to pay a loan to the tune of Rs.70 lacs.
Respondents No.3 & 4 further agreed to take appropriate steps for obtaining permission from the DIC for change of name for the aforesaid factories.

After execution of the said agreement, it came to the notice of the Complainant that Respondents No.1 to 4 have concealed the material facts that they could not transfer the ownership of factories within 5 years and have not deposited the premium amount from the period commencing from 2011 to 2015 because of which, the competent authority has cancelled the lease vide order dated 03.12.2015.
Thus, Respondents No.1 to 4 have cheated the Petitioners and the Petitioners have approached the police for registering FIR on 29.08.2015, but no action was taken

, therefore, the Petitioners have filed an application under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C before the JMFC and vide impugned order dated 26.03.2016, the JMFC, Durg has rejected the aforesaid application, which was also affirmed by the revisional Court.
Hence this Petition.

3. Shri Dhurandhar submits that from the contents of the complaint, offence under Section 420,
467, 471 and 120-B IPC was clearly made out against Respondents No.1 to 4, however, the police has neither registered the FIR nor made any enquiry in violation of the principles laid down in the matter of Lalita Kumari vs. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others reported in (2014) 2 SCC 1.

entities.text: Lalita Kumari vs. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Others reported in (2014) 2 SCC 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
He further submits that Respondents No.1 to 4 are not competent to execute the agreement dated 03.06.2014 and suppressing the material facts, they have cheated the Petitioners and the JMFC,
Durg has, in a mechanical manner, rejected the application filed under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C and the revisional Court has also not appreciated the facts in its true perspective and therefore, prays to quash the impugned orders by allowing the application filed under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C and directing the concerned authorities to register FIR against Respondents No.1 to 4.
4.
Per contra, Shri Agrawal, Senior Advocate supports the impugned order.

5. Learned State Counsel also submits that in the agreement dated 03.06.2014, it has been mentioned in a mechanical manner that there is an outstanding loan amount of Rs.70 lacs and it is the responsibility of the Petitioners to repay the same, therefore, there is no mala fide intention on the part of Respondents No.1 to 4 for which, the police has rightly not taken any cognizance.

6. Heard learned Counsel for the parties and perused the documents annexed with the Petition with utmost circumspection.
7.

In the matter of Priyanka Srivastava and Another vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Others reported in (2015) 6 SCC 287, in para-29 it has been categorically observed as under:-
"29. .....power under Section 156(3) warrants application of judicial mind.

entities.text: Priyanka Srivastava and Another vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Others reported in (2015) 6 SCC 287
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A court of law is involved.
It is not the police taking steps at the stage of Section 154 of the code.
A litigant at his own whim cannot invoke the authority of the Magistrate.
A principled and really grieved citizen with clean hands must have free access to invoke the said power.
It protects the citizens but when pervert litigations takes this route to harass Teeka Ram Chandel vs Anis on 20 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76709436/

2 their fellows citizens, efforts are to be made to scuttle and curb the same."
8.
Considering the aforesaid principles, in order to apply Section 420 IPC, namely cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property, the ingredients of Section 415 of the IPC have to be satisfied.

To constitute an offence of cheating under Section 415 IPC, a person should be induced,
either fraudulently or dishonestly to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property.
The second class of acts set forth in the section is the intentional inducement of doing or omitting to do anything which the person deceived would not do or omit to do, if she were not so deceived.

Thus, the sine qua non of Section 415 of the IPC is "fraudulence",
"dishonesty", or "intentional inducement", and the absence of these elements would debase the offence of cheating.

Explaining the contours, Supreme Court in Mohd. Ibrahim vs. State of Bihar reported in (2009) 8 SCC 751 observed that "for the offence of cheating, there should not only be cheating, but as a consequence of such cheating, the accused should also have dishonestly induced the person deceived to deliver any property to a person; or to make, alter, or destroy, wholly or in part, a valuable security, or anything signed or sealed and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security."

entities.text: Mohd. Ibrahim vs. State of Bihar reported in (2009) 8 SCC 751
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
9. In view of the aforesaid principles, after examining the facts of the present case, it is evident that in the agreement entered into by Respondents No.1 to 4 with the Petitioners on 03.06.2014, it has been categorically mentioned that both the factories are running on lease, which was granted by DIC and further, it was also mentioned therein that Respondents N.2, 3 & 4 have to take appropriate steps for change of name and after disclosing such material facts, the Petitioners have voluntarily agreed to the terms and entered into the agreement and paid a consideration to tune of Rs.21,24,000/- and were also ready and willing to take over the said factories which were in debt for loan of Rs.70 lacs and with the consent of the Petitioners, the concerned Bank had completed the necessary formalities and transferred the loan in the name of the Petitioners, therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that there is no fraud, dishonesty or intentional inducement on the part of the said Respondents and the JMFC, Durg has properly verified the nature of transaction and the allegation made in the application filed under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C, therefore, the order impugned whereby the application filed by the Petitioners was dismissed, is just and proper and does not call for any interference invoking the jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.PC.
10. Resultantly, the Petition being bereft of any merits, is hereby dismissed.
